transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-30
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Martinez (Redwood SE), Rachel Kim (CTO, Meridian), Marcus Lee (Platform), Sanjay Rao (Security), Olivia Park (ML)

Summary: quick POC scoping to align on private networking options (VPC peering vs AWS PrivateLink), region/residency constraints, egress controls, target workloads for benchmarking, and success criteria/timebox for a 4-week pilot. Customer emphasized strict egress auditing and corporate firewall that blocks unknown outbound endpoints.

Topics: success criteria; workload sizing (QPS, token lengths); benchmark plan (tail latency p95/p99, throughput); network topology options; KMS/data residency; timeline and next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00:02] Aisha (Redwood): Hey everyone — thanks for joining. Quick intros and then we'll jump into the topology options.
[00:00:10] Rachel (Meridian): Hi, Rachel here. We run clinical inference pipelines, low latency interactive UI for clinicians and batch reports overnight. Main ask: any patient data must never leave eu-west-1 and controls on egress.
[00:00:25] Marcus: And for sizing: typical peak is about 140 concurrent UI sessions, each about 300 tokens per request on average, spikes up to 350 qps for short bursts. Batch jobs hit large context windows but run off hours.
[00:00:35] Diego (Redwood): Got it — that's helpful. To confirm, region lock to eu-west-1 for inference and S3 residency too?
[00:00:42] Rachel: Yes, all PHI and derivative artifacts stay in eu-west-1. We can have control plane in other regions if needed, but must be auditable and use customer-managed KMS.
[00:00:52] Sanjay: Also we need full packet egress logs and ability to block outbound connections except approved endpoints.
[00:01:00] Aisha: Understood. We'll outline two main connectivity patterns: VPC peering (straight IP-level connection) and AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints). Each has tradeoffs we should review.
[00:01:12] Olivia: And performance impact? PrivateLink sometimes adds hop, right?
[00:01:17] Diego: Yeah, in our experience peering tends to have lower latency because it's direct L3 routing, PrivateLink goes through ENIs and can add a few milliseconds. But PrivateLink gives tighter egress control and simpler security posture — fewer route table changes, plus no cross-account route exposure.
[00:01:33] Marcus: For us, p95 latency for UI is the big metric. If PrivateLink adds 6–10 ms but keeps us compliant, that might be acceptable. What's realistic p95 numbers?
[00:01:44] Diego: For the model sizes you described (we're assuming a mid-sized LLM for embeddings/ranking and a larger for generation), baseline intra-region p95 token latency for gen path is around 120–220ms for 256 tokens on our optimized runtime. Network adds are often sub-20ms with peering; PrivateLink can add 5–15ms depending on path and ENI placement.
[00:02:05] Rachel: Okay. Our success criteria — to make it concrete: p95 end-to-end for 256-token interactive calls under 350ms, sustained throughput 200 concurrent sessions during peak, and no egress to public IPs (only to approved Redwood endpoints). Audit logs for every request with KMS envelope metadata.
[00:02:21] Aisha: That's a great clear set of success criteria — we'll map those to the benchmark plan.

[00:02:33] Diego: Now on benchmarking steps: suggest three phases — baseline (small sample model to validate connectivity and KV cache behavior), load test (simulate 200 concurrent UI sessions, realistic token distribution), and a security/egress verification run where customer inspects logs and we confirm no unexpected endpoints. We'll need sample payloads and an S3 bucket in eu-west-1 for test data.
[00:02:55] Marcus: We'll provide sample token histograms — short/medium/long — and two representative prompts: clinician summary (200–400 tokens) and report generation (1k+ tokens).
[00:03:06] Diego: Perfect. For load profile, we'll target 140 sustained with spikes to 350 for 30s windows. Also we'll instrument KV cache hit rates since prefix reuse will affect effective cost.

[00:03:22] Sanjay: On KMS, we want customer-managed CMKs in our account and limit Redwood's access to decrypt calls with envelope keys. Can you support that?
[00:03:30] Aisha: Yes — we support customer-managed KMS in the private deployment model and for Dedicated plans. For Hosted/PrivateLink we'll need a cross-account IAM role with limited decrypt permissions; we'll send our recommended policy.
[00:03:43] Rachel: Hmm, cross-account roles are doable but we need to justify in our audits. Any alternatives?
[00:03:48] Diego: If you run Redwood Private in your VPC (on-prem style or VPC-hosted private control plane), you keep full KMS control. That's heavier lift operationally but aligns with strict residency.

[00:03:59] Olivia: Can we clarify the difference again between PrivateLink and running Redwood Private inside our VPC?
[00:04:05] Aisha: Sure — PrivateLink keeps Redwood's inference runtime in Redwood-managed accounts but opens an interface endpoint in your VPC; network traffic to inference goes over the endpoint so data doesn't traverse the public internet. Redwood Private is where we deploy control and runtime into your environment (customer-managed) — that gives you more control over KMS, VPC flow logs, and placement, but requires more setup and an ops handoff.

[00:04:24] Marcus: For timelines, what's the typical effort for a 4-week pilot using PrivateLink vs full private deploy?
[00:04:31] Diego: PrivateLink pilot: 1–2 weeks to set up VPC endpoint and security reviews, then 1–2 weeks of benchmarking and tuning — total 3–4 weeks. Full private deploy tends to be 4–8 weeks depending on firewall changes and air-gapped approvals.
[00:04:45] Rachel: We are trying to get something live for a product evaluation in 5 weeks, so PrivateLink looks more realistic. But our security team may still demand KMS control which complicates things.

[00:04:56] Sanjay: If we do PrivateLink, we need to ensure that only specific subnets/instances can reach the endpoint and that logs are forwarded to our SIEM. Also we need egress to S3 to stay in eu-west-1 and be via VPC endpoints only.
[00:05:08] Diego: We can provide a recommended VPC design: dedicated subnets for inference clients, PrivateLink endpoint in a secure subnet with endpoint policy limiting which principals can connect. We'll also provide CloudWatch/Flow Log patterns we use for egress auditing.

[00:05:22] Olivia: One other thing — model pinning and rollbacks: in a POC we want to be able to pin a specific model and version for the runs to avoid drift. How do rollouts work in PrivateLink flow?
[00:05:32] Aisha: Model pinning is supported; rollouts are controlled via our Console or API. For PrivateLink, we expose the same API surface so you can pin model versions and we can do canary rollouts inside the pilot window. We'll log model-version metadata in request traces for your audits.

[00:05:46] Marcus: For the benchmark metrics we need: p50/p95/p99 latency, token/sec throughput, cost per 1k tokens (approx), and KV cache hit ratio. Also memory/GPU utilization for the reserved capacity nodes if possible.
[00:06:00] Diego: We'll surface GPU utilization and per-request cost estimations from the runtime. For the pilot we'll run synthetic traffic and share a spreadsheet with p95/p99 and cost extrapolations.

[00:06:14] Aisha: Let's build a minimal acceptance checklist for the POC: 1) p95 < 350ms for 256-token interactive calls; 2) sustain 200 concurrent sessions at target token distribution; 3) zero outbound to non-approved IPs during the security run; 4) KMS/envelope key metadata present in logs; 5) runbook for failover if a region is unhealthy. Agree?
[00:06:33] Rachel: Yes that maps well. We'll add one: audit logs retained for 90 days during pilot.
[00:06:39] Sanjay: And we want a short playbook for rollback to our previous synchronous inference path in case latencies or costs spike.

[00:06:48] Diego: Noted — we'll include a rollback playbook with traffic cutover steps.

[00:06:55] Aisha: I also want to call out egress nuances: if you have NAT gateways, make sure the NAT's IPs are whitelisted for any external telemetry endpoints we need to reach. For full isolation, PrivateLink plus interface endpoints to S3/KMS keep traffic internal.
[00:07:08] Marcus: We do use NATs now for some monitoring egress — our security team wants minimal exceptions.
[00:07:13] Olivia: For the tests, can Redwood run a localized KV cache warm-up to simulate real traffic patterns? Cold starts are killing for us.
[00:07:20] Diego: Absolutely — we'll include a warmup phase and measure cold vs warm p95/p99. We'll also instrument cache hit rates so you can see real savings.

[00:07:34] Rachel: About data residency: the outputs from the model — summaries and derived features — are they stored anywhere outside eu-west-1 in your hosted variant?
[00:07:41] Aisha: For hosted, telemetry and some control-plane logs currently live in our control region — but payloads and model outputs can be configured to stay in eu-west-1 as part of the PrivateLink pilot. For more strict needs, Redwood Private keeps everything in your region. We'll mark this as a blocker for SOC evidence.
[00:07:57] Sanjay: We'll need a statement of data flow diagram for our auditors. Can you provide that with network hops and KMS usage?
[00:08:04] Aisha: Yes we'll provide a network/data flow diagram and an annex for KMS and log retention.

[00:08:14] Marcus: On the technical deep dive — any specific tuning we should know for long-context batch jobs? They need to run overnight and shouldn't compete with the interactive tier.
[00:08:22] Diego: We recommend two approaches: isolate batch on dedicated capacity pools (Dedicated or a reserved pool) or schedule off-peak with autoscaling policies. For KV cache and memory pressure, long contexts increase memory usage: we'll size GPUs accordingly in the pilot. We'll run a small memory/throughput benchmark to recommend instance types.

[00:08:40] Rachel: Cost visibility is important — include token-level cost and an estimate per 1k tokens for our expected distribution.
[00:08:46] Aisha: We'll include a cost model and an expected monthly run-rate for your workload shapes.

[00:08:55] Diego: Quick note on fallback during outages: we can set routing policies to fall back to a smaller model or a different region — but if region lock is mandatory, fallback isn't possible unless you allow cross-region capacity. We'll document tradeoffs.
[00:09:08] Rachel: We want graceful degradation but only within eu-west-1. So smaller model fallback is fine but can't cross regions.

[00:09:16] Olivia: Any security approvals we should expect from Redwood for PrivateLink — like penetration test reports?
[00:09:22] Aisha: We can share SOC2 Type II report and a summary of our pen test cycles. For PrivateLink specifics we can share config examples and endpoint policies.

[00:09:33] Marcus: Ok so action-oriented ask: Diego, please produce the network diagram and a recommended subnet/route table config. Aisha, send the compliance artifacts. We'll provide sample workloads and token distributions by next Monday. Then schedule the benchmark window for week of July 13th.
[00:09:50] Aisha: Sounds good. We'll also propose an initial 2-hour benchmark slot and a 4-week pilot timeline doc.

[00:09:58] Sanjay: One last question — telemetry: can logs be exported to our SIEM in near real time?
[00:10:04] Diego: Yes, CloudWatch/Flow Logs can be forwarded, and request traces can be exported to your preferred collector. We'll include a recommended logging stream design.

[00:10:13] Rachel: Great. I think that's it for the main items.

[00:10:18] Aisha: Thank you everyone — we'll send the artifacts and proposed dates. Recap of next steps in the follow-up.

[00:10:25] (conversation winds down, small scheduling chat)
[00:11:10] [Call end — rest of the recording is short outro and calendar follow-up scheduling dialogue]

Notes on transcript quality: occasional misrecognitions (e.g., some product names and acronyms may be slightly off). Shared artifacts mentioned: private-link-vs-peering-diagram.pdf (link sent in chat), meridian-sample-token-histogram.csv (customer to share), redwood-soc2-summary.pdf (Redwood to send).

Benchmark plan (brief):
- Week 0 (prep): exchange configs, KMS/endpoint permissions, test S3 bucket in eu-west-1.
- Week 1: PrivateLink setup + connectivity validation + baseline latency tests (cold and warm).
- Week 2: Load tests — simulate 140 sustained, spikes to 350, measure p50/p95/p99; KV cache instrumentation.
- Week 3: Security run — egress verification, SIEM ingestion test, KMS proof-of-access checks.
- Post-run: analysis and cost extrapolation delivered in spreadsheet.

Acceptance criteria (POC):
- p95 end-to-end for 256 tokens < 350ms
- sustain 200 concurrent UI sessions matching token distribution
- zero unexpected egress destinations observed during security run
- KMS envelope metadata present and auditable
- 90-day log retention for pilot period

End of transcript.
